half-duplex wireless network consisting of N nodes, where each node can communicate with at most one other node for a specific time slot.  A key problem, that of finding optimal cooperation strategies, has been fully resolved for N ≤ 4.  However, for N ≥ 5, the problem becomes significantly more complex due to the exponential number of possible configurations.  Building upon recent breakthroughs in similar, yet less complex, information-theoretic problems, we develop novel graphical representations - specifically, a combination of intersection graphs and pairing graphs - to model the communication schedule as a process of bonding and breaking edges and pairing vertices.  By employing these representations, we derived optimal strategies for N = 5 and N = 6 through a combination of problem-specific arguments and general graphical theory principles.  The obtained strategies achieve the fundamental limits of the network's throughput and the signal-to-interference-ratio at these point values, outperforming previous known optima.  The most desirable throughputs for N = 5 and N = 6 are 6/7 and 8/9 respectively, which are also shown to be universally achievable.  This represents the first instance where the fundamental limits of the network's throughput and the signal-to-interference-ratio have been precisely defined for N ≥ 5.  This research lays the groundwork for future studies on larger network sizes.  One of the key contributions includes establishing the maximum average throughput of at most 2/3 for each user, which occurs when each node participates in exactly two communications.  Additionally, this research provides a framework for solving other similar problems within similar network configurations, which can be further explored in various variations of two-way half-duplex wireless networks.  This includes, but is not limited to, extending the study to three-dimensional space, varying node densities, and exploring different performance metrics.  This paper's findings on the fundamental limits of the network's throughput and the signal-to-interference-ratio for N = 5 and N = 6 are also extendable to more complex scenarios such as linear arrays and nonuniform node distributions.  This research on the fundamental limits of the network's throughput and the signal-to-interference-ratio in two-dimensional two-way half-duplex wireless networks paves the way for various applications across multiple fields of study.  This includes, but is not limited to, noncooperative spectrum sharing, cooperative ALOHA protocols, relay channels, and cognitive radio networks. We investigate how the alignment of neutron star spin axes affects the shape of gravitational waves, using an effective hydrodynamic theory that incorporates binary neutron star system dynamics.  Through a linearized analysis of the hydrodynamic theory, we find that the phase difference between the waveforms generated by nonrelativistic, tidally locked neutron stars is solely determined by the angular separation of their spin axes.  Specifically, we find that the phase difference is directly proportional to the product of the stars' momenta of inertia and the tidal coupling constant, and inversely proportional to the frequency difference between the stars' orbital and spin periods.  This phase difference relationship holds true regardless of the stars' mass ratios, as long as the binary system is nonrelativistic and the stars are tidally locked.  By further analyzing the hydrodynamic theory, we identify the key source of gravitational waves as oscillations in the stellar triaxiality, driven by the tidal force.  We conclude that the linearized theory accurately represents the conservative dynamics of binary neutron star systems, and provides a framework for understanding how the alignment of neutron star spin axes influences the shape of gravitational waves.  We also outline the applicability of this analysis to both nonrelativistic and post-Newtonian approaches.  Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the search of binary neutron star-induced phenomena in gravitational wave observations, and the potential for using these effects as beacons for identifying the orientation of neutron stars.  We further explore the possibility of utilizing these effects in the analysis of future gravitational wave data, and its potential to drive the discovery of new phenomena in astrophysics.  We have made the code used in these computations available online, along with a Python implementation of the linearized theory. This paper presents our findings from using low-quality data to train and test object detection models, with the aim of exploring the robustness of such models.  We demonstrate that errors occurring when processing datasets may affect model performance, and that noise injection could provide a solution to some issues, albeit with decreased performance.  Our research suggests that supervised models are not inherently robust to data quality flaws, contradicting previous claims.  We also contribute several key findings, including the discovery that noise injection is ineffective against errors caused by binning and that linear boundary functions are more resilient than their nonlinear counterparts.  These findings provide valuable guidance on the design of boundary functions for binning errors and the potential for future research into more effective approaches.  The proposed method outperforms existing strategies in noise simulations and real-world image experiments, demonstrating its potential for use in real systems.  Our simplest proposed boundary function model achieves an average precision of 0.8 in noise simulations and 9.3% improvement over the baseline in a real-world image experiment.  This research has important implications for the design of object detection systems and the development of robust boundary function models. In a proposed technique, adversarially trained GANs are used to create perturbed examples that aim to evade detection by classification models trained to recognize embedded patterns or biases in data.  Contrary to the intent of fairness monitoring models, these GAN-based approaches have been shown to introduce new biases into results, according to studies published in ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability and Transparency 2023. $\gamma$ decays of nuclei have been extensively used to probe shell structure, particularly in medium to heavy mass regions.  Theoretical models, such as the Nuclear Density Functional Theory, rely on these decay patterns to validate their stability against pairing correlations.  The odd-even nucleon shelf, a hallmark of pairings in nuclei, is a key indicator of this structure.  With the advent of advanced radioactive beam facilities, there is growing interest in probing light nuclei for possible pairings, given their previously unexplored decay patterns. QCD leads to a complex description, particularly when it comes to lattice simulations.  As a result, researchers often resort to approximations like the mean-field limit, which may miss essential aspects of the theory, especially those related to flavor symmetry breaking and the appearance of diquark masses.  A non-perturbative approach that overcomes this limitation is truly essential.  A framework that truly meets this criterion is the functional renormalization group, particularly suitable for studying hot quark matter.  Building upon previous research, particularly in [1] and [2], we aim to investigate the breaking of symmetry and the formation of diquark masses within a modified MRG flow approximation.  This approximation proves highly effective in resolving the complex structure of gap equations, allowing for a precise determination of critical temperatures.  Specifically, we find consistent results with other approaches concerning the breaking of symmetry for two massless flavors, as well as the formation of diquark masses for three flavors, with approximately $2.06$ times more massive antisymmetric than symmetric diquarks.  Furthermore, we observe a direct correlation between the formation of diquark masses and the appearance of density-driven vacuum structure in the $0++$ and $1-$ channels.  This thorough analysis provides a solid foundation for investigating the phase diagram of a system comprising two light flavors and a third heavier flavor, with possible applications to QCD-like theories and theories of dense quark matter.  Specifically, we can derive a minimum mass threshold of approximately $200$MeV for strange quarks in a system comprising two light flavors, as well as a phase diagram that showcases the formation of diquark masses with increasing density and temperature for a system comprising two light flavors and a third heavier flavor, with a minimum formation temperature of approximately $50$MeV for antisymmetric diquarks.  Lastly, we find a formation density of approximately $10^{-3}$fm$^{-3}$ for symmetric diquarks in a system comprising two light flavors and a third heavier flavor.  This comprehensive study paves the way for future studies, particularly those concerning the inclusion of electromagnetic interactions and the extension to theories with multiple fermion species.  Additionally, we include a set of valuable numerical tables and figures at the end of the document for further analysis.  Finally, we make the code publicly available to facilitate the reproduction of results and future research.  This overall approach truly enables a precise, non-perturbative understanding of diquark formation mechanisms in QCD-like theories

of systems known as linear systems with dynamic constraints, where the dynamics of a part of the system are unknown and only provide limited information.  Unlike previous studies, we incorporate a key novelty - a constraint on the rate of change of the unknown dynamics.  A control strategy is developed that uses the measured information about the unknown dynamics efficiently, demonstrating the system's ability to be stabilized around a target state.  Furthermore, we derive conditions that the system must satisfy to be stabilizable, showing that the constraint on the rate of change is crucial for a system to be stabilized in the first place.  A specific example is provided to illustrate the application of these conditions.  By leveraging a linear structure, we can incorporate the constraint as a boundary within a convex domain, facilitating the use of linear matrix inequalities to analyze the system's stability.  Essentially, we are enclosing the unknown dynamics within a fixed, though potentially large, bound, which might not be the most optimal scenario.  However,, as shown by Jarrett, Lessmann, and Tabuada (2019), a more tight wrapping is possible by employing a moving bound that adapts to the system's behavior.  Specifically, they introduced the concept of a "barrier variable" that can be utilized to define a tighter, possibly nonconvex region of stability.  We build upon their idea, presenting an alternative representation utilizing a linear structure that is more efficient than the "double polyhedral" shape.  By employing a "diagonal polyhedral" shape, we can further improve the stability bounds, potentially leading to more efficient control strategies. We find that the X-ray and jet spectra can be fit with a single electron energy distribution index of about 1.2, indicating that the jet is relativistic.  We use radiative acceleration theory to explain why the jet remains relativistic, despite its large observed luminosity compared to the host galaxy's luminosity.  We also use the same model to show that the jet's speed should be close to the speed of light at the injection point, likely within a fraction of a century after the massive star's explosion.  We propose a possible scenario in which the blastwave breaks through the circumstellar wind created by the massive star's mass loss, leading to the jet's observed behavior.  We use the fit parameters to calculate the jet's opening angle and relativistic beaming factor at ~10^4 s after the burst, finding that the host galaxy GB090729-054137 should be visible in optical observations.  We confirm this by the detection of the galaxy by the HST.  We conclude that GRB 090717A was a long-duration, wide-angle GRB similar to GRB 060923A. Although numerous algorithms have been developed to recognize music notation, this research aims to enhance the precision of OMR systems by introducing a post-processing phase that focuses on resolving ambiguities in note identification. A full theoretical treatment was applied to an open $N$-particle system, in contrast to the typical use of the $K$-sector reduced density matrix for analysis. A driving force was applied to the system's ends to create a particle flow. The key findings include: (1) the steady-state particle flow can be precisely described using the concept of chemical potentials; (2) the system's behavior was found to transition from a coherent to a incoherent flow regime as the driving force increased; (3) the role of interactions among particles was analyzed, revealing its influence on the flow's characteristics; and (4) the theoretical model was validated by conducting a particle conservation validation. This study focuses on the 250-um dust emission maps that feature a sensitivity of 2.7millijans per 50x50 arcsec^2 pixels.  Within the central 10kpc of M51, we identified a total of 761 dust disk detection patterns, which were further categorized into three groups: main, secondary, and tertiary disks.  An examination of the detection patterns reveals a power-law distribution for both massive (M > 10^5 M_sun) and less massive (~10^3 M_sun < M <= 10^5 M_sun) disks.  However, when adjusting for disk radius, the distribution becomes linear.  Notably, we observed a significant dearth of massive disks in the 1-10^4 M_sun mass range, which we attribute to the simultaneous detection of disk properties via 24.5um and Halpha data.  An analysis of the disk scale heights revealed a negative power-law relationship with respect to both mass and stellar surface density, indicating that disk thickness diminishes as it becomes more massive or dense.  Finally, we observed a positive correlation between disk scale heights and radius, which is consistent with the theory that disk flaring is driven by the balance between stellar gravity and radiation pressure.  Based on the analysis, we propose a model that links dust disk thickness to the local stellar environment, which can be used to predict the scale heights of disks with masses between 10^3 and 10^6 M_sun and radii between 10 and 1000pc.  This model is poised to contribute significantly to our understanding of dust disk evolution and its role in planetary formation processes.  Ultimately, this study paves the way for a more comprehensive, three-dimensional model of dust disk structure, which the author plans to develop in a forthcoming paper.  This research also serves as a foundation for a series of upcoming studies on specific dust disk systems within M51, which will explore the relationship between dust disk evolution and the formation of gas giant planets. This work explores the feasibility of directly processing binary data such as images in their raw, uncompressed format within integrated circuits.  To achieve this, we've developed a family of arithmetic circuits that can perform computations on binary data at the bit-level, allowing for more creative design possibilities for systems that process images on the fly.  A protocol for combining multiple operations and a method for representing comparison outcomes have also been established.  By implementing these circuits using field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs), we've created a system that can perform image filtering on the fly, demonstrating the viability of this approach for hardware designers.  The designs are open-source, available on an online repository, and can serve as a foundation for developing more complex image processing systems.  The design's flexibility is showcased by processing different images using various filters, and its potential is demonstrated by implementing a sophisticated image smoothing algorithm.  The overall goal is to pave the way for designing innovative image processing systems that prioritize performance, area, and power constraints.  To this end, we've thoroughly analyzed the costs associated with implementing different circuit components and have identified several key findings.  The most significant contribution is a set of performance benchmarks for various bit-level operation templates that serve as a blueprint for designing new systems.  The benchmarks reveal a positive linear relationship between the number of bit operations required and the growth in area and power consumption, as well as a quadratic relationship with the increase in delay time.  The benchmarks can also be used to calculate the overall performance of systems that perform multiple operations in succession, demonstrating its utility in processing a filter that masks values in images.  The overall aim is to establish a framework for hardware designers to evaluate the efficacy of their ideas and to provide a foundation for developing more sophisticated image processing systems. pandemic's impact on economic activity have led to disparate estimates of government intervention's effectiveness in promoting economic activity.  To resolve this variation, we employ a unified framework that integrates context and outcomes, enabling a precise assessment of the representativeness of included data.  Using European country-data from 2019 to 2021, we find that lockdowns and other government measures delay economic recovery but ultimately boost overall activity.  Furthermore, we observe significant cross-country variation in response intensity and timing, which correlates with factors such as demographic composition, mobility, and virus transmission rates.  By accounting for context and outcomes, we can determine that measures targeting high-risk populations and activities most vulnerable to transmission are more likely to be effective, which supports targeted policy approaches.  Ultimately, our findings support the use of lockdowns and other government interventions as tools to control the virus and promote economic activity, which is in contrast to the concerns about their efficacy expressed in some previous studies.  The results also provide valuable insights for developing data-driven pandemic mitigation strategies.  To facilitate this, we have made our code and data available for researchers.  Additionally, we propose an open-data platform to monitor and respond to future public health crises.  This platform would feature real-time economic and context-data for various countries and regions, which would be invaluable for evaluating the effectiveness of government interventions and informing policy decisions.  This proposed platform is particularly relevant given the widespread lockdowns and other government measures that were implemented worldwide in response to the Omicron variant of the virus at the end of 2021.  This paper's findings and recommendations contribute to the growing body of research on the subject, which includes studies on the impact of government interventions on employment outcomes, consumer behavior, and specific industries, as well as analyses of the effects of lockdowns on air pollution and wildlife populations.  This paper's unique perspective and methods also provide a framework for evaluating the effectiveness of government policies in response to future public health crises.  This includes the potential use of targeted measures to control the spread of infectious diseases, the potential consequences of lockdowns on vulnerable populations, and the potential benefits of government support for businesses and individuals affected by lockdowns.  This paper's findings and recommendations can also be applied to evaluating the effectiveness of government policies in response to other external shocks, such as natural disasters and global conflicts, which can help inform the development of resilience strategies.  This paper's unified framework for evaluating the effectiveness of government interventions can be applied across various fields, including economics, public health, and environmental science,

Despite the solved structures of numerous proteins, approximately half of their total number remain unknown due to the limitations of experimental methods. In an effort to address these challenges, advanced computational methods such as metadynamics allow for the simulation of protein conformational changes and the reconstruction of their associated free energy landscapes. With the growing accessibility of high-performance computing, nonequilibrium metadynamics is poised to make a significant impact on protein simulation studies, potentially leading to breakthroughs in our understanding of protein function and behavior. In a single simulation, this method can facilitate the transition of proteins between distinct conformational states, eliminating the need to prespecify reaction coordinates. What follows is a detailed description of nonequilibrium metadynamics theory, its practical application, and a series of benchmarks. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of time-dependent nonequilibrium metadynamics in simulating protein conformational changes, outperforming traditional biasing techniques.

Unlike traditional methods that rely on statistical knowledge of the signal, this solution employs a machine learning network at each sensor to resolve the problem.  A key component of this system is a neural discriminator, which learns how to distinguish between signal and noise within each individual sensor's data stream.  Once the discriminator is trained, it can determine the signal presence at each sensor, allowing the overall learner to calculate the sources' parameters.  A key finding is that, in an ideal environment, the sources' parameters can be determined as accurately as possible using a single signal mixture version, and multiple mixture versions can be combined to further improve resolution.  However, when noise corruption affects the environment, signal loss can occur in the source parameter spectra, potentially leading to a reduction in overall dimensionality.  To address this, the authors developed a convex optimization algorithm to reconstruct the lost resolution, which proved particularly effective when mixture versions were plentiful but offered limited benefits otherwise.  As the method solves a fundamental problem in signal processing, potential applications include imaging and data reconstruction in physics.  In an example using two sources with distinct parameters (signal-to-noise ratios of 20 and 10 dB), a single mixture version with an SNR of 20 dB was sufficient to resolve both fully, and adding multiple mixture versions offered increasing resolution without sacrificing shape integrity.  When noise levels varied between the sources, multiple mixture versions were essential for recovering both profiles completely, and one version with an SNR of 20 dB was insufficient but sufficient when a version with an SNR of 15 dB was added.  When multiple mixture versions were available, the optimization algorithm contributed significantly to overall resolution, but when versions were scarce, it offered limited benefits.  In another example using two sources with severely disparate parameters (SNRs of 30 and 0 dB), a single mixture version with an SNR of 20 dB was sufficient to recover both profiles fully, but when versions were scarce, the optimization algorithm was ineffective.  In an example using three sources with distinct parameters (SNRs of 20, 15, and 10 dB), multiple mixture versions were necessary to recover all three profiles completely, and a single version with an SNR of 20 dB was insufficient but sufficient when a version with an SNR of 15 dB was added. As these phenomena manifest as rare changes in data, preserving the integrity of signal processing is paramount. We examine the theoretical connection between astroparticle detectors and signal processing techniques, specifically the integration trade-off in parameter estimation, which is analogous to the noise floor in signal processing. By applying the Fisher information matrix, we can optimize the parameter estimation capability of these systems, and a minimum bound emerges that is independent of how the estimation problem is posed. This bound corresponds to the optimal performance that can be achieved with an underlying processing system, and it serves as a barometer for determining the necessity of system upgrades. As an example, we apply this framework to a next-generation ground-based dark matter detector, and it demonstrates that an order of magnitude improvement in sensitivity is potentially possible by upgrading the gas gain in the detection technology. Unlike typical situations, where invariant sets are known or assumed, this work examines cases where the form of these invariants is unknown. A new method, called the 'Symplectic Reduction' technique, is introduced and demonstrated to be particularly effective for identifying invariant tori in such complex systems. The approach is then applied to two specific physical models: a rotating gravity-driven pendulum and a precessing magnetic dipole. In both cases, the technique yielded novel invariants that directly factorized into the form preferred for hamiltonian reduction, thereby facilitating a more intuitive understanding of the system's dynamics. droplets to stick and spread, and their behavior is often described using the contact angle. However, its measurement is prone to inaccuracy when the drop's shape deviates significantly from the equilibrium state. Furthermore, it solely provides information about the liquid's margin, missing details on the drop's interior and spreading dynamics. In contrast, computer simulations can precisely capture both the drop's shape and contact angle but rely on validated models of the non-wetting substrate's behavior. Thus, a realistic description of non-wetting phenomena requires a proper understanding of the substrate's fluid dynamics, especially in complex scenarios. In response, we develop a novel, effective capillary pressure model for non-wetting substrates, focusing on steady, non-relaxational flow conditions. The new model expands on the traditional interface-based approach by introducing a dynamic contact line and accounting for the Serrin-Birkhoff theorem to ensure the conservation of mass. Additionally, it eliminates the need for a precursor film, allowing for a more realistic description of the liquid-substrate interface. We demonstrate the model's validity by simulating typical non-wetting scenarios and compare its performance to an existing interface-based model. The results show that the new model reduces the contact angle hysteresis and more accurately describes spreading and receding dynamics. Moreover, it can be easily coupled with the Shan-Chen pseudopotential lattice Boltzmann method to simulate non-wetting phenomena on rough surfaces. Finally, we apply the new model to investigate the impact of a gas bubble on a non-wetting substrate and observe distinct behavior based on the initial bubble velocity. The overall aim is to provide a robust, practical framework for simulating non-wetting phenomena on complex substrates through an improved capillary pressure model.

In response, search engines are incentivized to rank websites with high probability of attracting users' interest highly, hoping these users will click on relevant ads shortly after searching. While this approach may benefit search engines financially, it raises concerns about the potential manipulation of search engine rankings by SNS providers through their control over relevant content. In a 2016 paper, Mehra and Rosenberg observed that SNS providers like YouTube, Amazon, and Facebook are listed prominently when using general search terms, and they speculated that these providers might be using SNS-specific content to influence rankings. Building on this observation, this research investigates the possibility of SNS providers influencing search engine rankings through the strategic presentation of content, and it demonstrates that this is indeed an effective method. Specifically, researchers found that by creating niche content on the Wikipedia equivalent "Japanese" category in a subtopic "Tea" and linking it to a main article, they could make the subtopic appear in search results when using broad search terms related to the subtopic. This discovery led to several theoretical findings, and it contributes to our understanding of how search engine ranking algorithms can be exploited for commercial purposes. Furthermore, the paper presents several potential solutions to this issue, and it offers directions for future research. In addition, the authors provide a critique of existing laws and policy frameworks that govern search engine ranking regulation, and they propose new approaches to governing the optimization of search engine rankings. This paper investigates the potential technical limitations in the structure of recurrent neural networks that prevent them from learning basic grammatical concepts like punctuation. It presents a mathematical proof that standard recurrent neural networks cannot distinguish between punctuation marks, and an intuitive explanation of why this limitation occurs. It also explores possible solutions, and demonstrates the effectiveness of a simple training approach to teach punctuation knowledge using minimal data. The findings support the idea that the fundamental design of recurrent neural networks creates a barrier to learning about punctuation, and that a pre-trained model can fill this gap. This research contributes to a deeper understanding of the inner workings of ELMo and BERT models, and provides practical guidance on using them especially when working with plain text data.  This research demonstrates that ELMo context-dependent embeddings that ignore punctuation deliver comparable performance to context-dependent embeddings that preserve punctuation in multiple tasks, and outperforms context-independent embeddings in all tasks.  It also conducts an in-depth analysis of the advantages of using ELMo over BERT, and finds that it excels in situations where the model's internal workings greatly impact performance.  This research paves the way for developing a truly punctuation-agnostic character-level embedding scheme, and its potential applications include enhancing the consistency of tokenization and improving the accuracy of part-of-speech tagging. An approach from information theory allows us to define a society's value system in terms of the mutual information between scenarios, which represents the unexpected, revealing aspects of the system when the scenarios are unknown.  Building on this foundation, we can calculate the information density that normalizes and scales the value system, allowing for a unifying framework that integrates multiple principles.  By applying the information theory framework, we can analytically derive fair division methods for allocating resources, as well as computationally efficient algorithms for implementing these methods.  Specifically, we obtain novel, generative fair division algorithms for distributing multiple resources among multiple groups, based on predefined majority standards, and a recursive algorithm for incorporating new, related values.  The information theory perspective enables a unified understanding of various fairness standards, including proportional, majority, and sequential majority fairness, as well as a general metric for evaluating the fairness of any joint distribution of values.  Furthermore, we can model value systems that prioritize complex value hierarchies, shift in perspective between different value-bearing entities, and account for the uncertainty in measuring values.  Rephrasing the society's value system as a matrix of information values allows us to apply various computational methods, including optimization problems, Markov chain Monte Carlo simulations, and the development of a value-based game theory.  The information theory framework provides a robust tool for analyzing and describing a society's value system, enabling the design of fair division mechanisms that reflect the underlying principles and values.  We believe that this approach holds significant potential for integrating value-based reasoning into artificial intelligence and multi-agent decision-making systems.  In an ideal world with perfectly known value systems, the information theory framework would lead to universally agreed-upon fair division outcomes.  However, the framework's resilience to noise in value measurements allows it to be highly effective in practical scenarios with imperfect value data.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of the information theory-based approach by conducting a series of computational experiments on various representative scenarios, including a large-scale real-world dataset from a fair division application on housing allocation among different racial groups in the United States.  The results show that the information theory-based approach can lead to significantly better fair division outcomes compared to other fairness standards, by accurately reflecting the underlying value system and incorporating complex value hierarchies.  The information theory framework provides a novel, unifying perspective on fairness standards in decision-making, allowing us to derive computationally efficient, mutually exclusive fairness algorithms for multiple standards.

cool, star-forming galaxies can either facilitate the formation of SNeIb/c or obscure their signature at gamma-ray observatories. The association of two supernovae, SN 2008D and its possible interaction with a nearby HII region, with a pre-existing large-scale density wave or a magnetic cavity offers a distinct perspective on this scenario. By analyzing the non-thermal radiation observed in SN 2008D, it is found that neither a wide, narrow, or combination of both density wave(s) can produce sufficient shock acceleration to radiative leptons. However, the inclusion of a magnetic field, oriented perpendicularly to the density wave, can bridge this gap and provide the necessary environment for the production of gamma-ray non-thermal radiation. This discovery suggests that large-scale magnetic fields play a crucial role in the conversion of supernova energy into gamma-rays. Moreover, it is found that the parameters of the shock, the density wave, and the magnetic field are in agreement with the microphysics of hadronic and leptonic gamma-ray production processes. This study's findings contribute to the growing body of evidence supporting the importance of magnetic fields in shaping the non-thermal radiation observed in SNeIb/c. It also highlights the potential of combined observational and theoretical analyses to refine our understanding of this phenomenon. Finally, it is recommended that future gamma-ray telescope missions, such as the Cerenkov Telescope Array, consider the presence of large-scale magnetic fields in the line-of-sight to SNeIb/c, particularly those occurring in dense, star-forming environments. As a pioneering detection method, it is crucial to accurately assess its sensitivity to the faint signal expected from the photon ring of an eclipse-like event. In a recent work, Massey and others found a limit of $10^{-9}$ in massless binary systems through the analysis of Einstein-Chandrasekhar accretion disk systems. However, we found that this limit is overly optimistic by several orders of magnitude through a detailed computational examination of the Einstein-Chandrasekhar accretion disk model. Specifically, we determined that a signal-to-noise ratio of 5 is only achievable for a binary system with a mass of $10^{2}$ solar masses through the analysis of the Einstein-Chandrasekhar radii through microlensing observations. Furthermore, we observed that the limit declines to a signal-to-noise ratio of around 3 for systems with a mass of $10^{3}$ solar masses. Additionally, we conducted a thorough investigation of various Einstein-Chandrasekhar models, including those of Shakura-Sunyaev and Slaný\v{r}ka-Novák, and found similar limits. Finally, we examined the influence of the photon ring's properties on the sensitivity of the microlensing technique and determined that it is largely unaffected by changes in the mass of the compact object and the wavelength of the observing spectrum. All in all, our results indicate that the current microlensing data offers little to no contribution towards the detection of the photon ring of an eclipse-like event through the analysis of the Einstein-Chandrasekhar accretion disk model. However, we believe that the technique holds significant potential in other eclipse-like events, such as those involving the massless binary system AGN PG 1241+689.

Building upon this setup, we have developed a strategy called "Shielded Control" that combines an observer, which attempts to accurately grasp the state of the environment, and a controller that makes informed decisions. Utilizing the Shielded Control framework in a discrete state space and an infinite state space were both explored.  In a discrete state space, we found that an ideal shield-free policy is reachable for any error probability. To counter this, we develop a protocol that employs a verified quantum majority vote, wherein multiple untrusted quantum devices are used in parallel, with their outputs merged through a simple verified quantum vote. Although the Néel temperature is a critical property for magnetic materials, there is a lack of comprehensive, theoretical predictions for magnetic interface properties. This paper aims to fill this gap by providing a comprehensive, theoretical analysis of magnetic interface properties at the interface between strontium titanate and manganite layers, (001)-oriented within an Ruddlesden-Popper structure. We investigate the possibility of relativistic jets in these events emitting X-rays through electron scattering of relativistic photons, following their own flow.  We performed 1D and 2D relativistic hydrodynamic simulations of GRB afterflows and analyzed the results.  We found that in the case of narrow, dense jets, the energy of relativistic electrons is sufficient for the process to occur, but it is not efficient due to the low energy density of relativistic photons.  On the other hand, we discovered that in the case of wide, thin jets, the energy of electrons is not sufficient; however, the process becomes possible thanks to the presence of relativistic photons within the jet.  We used the hydrodynamic simulation data to model the inverse Compton process and calculated the resulting X-ray spectra for both jet geometries.  For a standard injection index of $-2$, we found that the process leads to a flat X-ray spectrum for narrow jets and a rising spectrum for wide jets.  We also determined the product of the X-ray and radio luminosities to be approximately constant for both cases.  We conclude that the process of relativistic photon scattering constitutes a viable X-ray emission mechanism for powerful extragalactic lasers.  We further suggest that this process might be responsible for the observed X-ray luminosity peaks in GRBs and blazars.  Finally, we propose a unified theory of GRB and blazar behavior, placing the relativistic photon scattering process at its core.  We believe that this theory has the potential to reconcile various observed properties of GRBs and blazars.  We also outline several areas of interest for future research.  One such area involves investigating the variability patterns of GRBs and blazars through the relativistic photon scattering process.  Another area involves exploring the possibility of observing signatures of this process in the spectra of blazars.  We anticipate that further studies will help confirm the validity of our unified theory.  If verified, this theory could provide a fundamental understanding of powerful extragalactic lasers and their place within the broader context of relativistic jets. This method is designed to provide instantaneous, three-dimensional information about the particle cloud, allowing for real-time calculation of statistical quantities without the need for extensive precursor simulations. As these instabilities directly drive the transport of heat and particles, a thorough comprehension of their onset is crucial for both tokamak edge stability projects and stellarator confinement projects. Despite the critical importance of assessing the growth rates of shear helical magnetic instabilities, especially in overlaying curved and torsional geometry contexts, current local linear stability analysis techniques fall short. By utilizing this operator representation, we can assess the stability bounds of REI and CRET instabilities, as well as determine the instability growth rates in realistic configuration space, all within the local linear stability theory scope. By applying this scheme in global gyrofluid simulations and comparisons with the linear MHD stability code STEFICE-, we verified its validity. To evaluate the skill of these models in predicting climate patterns, we conduct a linear stability analysis of the climate system's representation in general circulation models.  By doing so, we identify the underlying dynamics that dictate the behavior of climate patterns, allowing us to classify them into two main categories:  persistent patterns and oscillatory modes.  We find that the linear growth or decay of these patterns is not an accurate indicator of their representability in models of various resolutions.  Instead, we determine that the critical lines of linear growth/decay in the model parameter space correspond to the Lagrange multipliers of an associated adjoint maximization problem, which we identify through a numerical alternative.  We believe that this theoretical framework can be applied to various GCMs and forcing scenarios, and we demonstrate its utility by investigating the stability conditions of the stratospheric polar vortex and the Northern Annular Mode in response to changes in solar radiation and carbon dioxide concentrations.  We observe that the linear stability analysis complements the traditional assessment of model performance through pattern persistence times, allowing us to evaluate the representability of climate patterns on the timescale of 20-50 years in GCMs of various resolutions.  We conclude that the linear stability analysis provides a practical tool for assessing the capability of GCMs to predict climate patterns on various timescales, which we hope will contribute to the development of more efficient climate simulation strategies. We created a tool that explores the distinction between neutron star and black hole systems, and it is available for use at http://lisa-star-blackhole.com.  This tool is pre-loaded with various equation of state models, and users can also input their own models.  We believe that LISA systems with masses less than about 1.5 solar masses will be identifiable as consisting of neutron stars, based on theoretical understanding of supernova explosion mechanisms and binary evolution pathways.  We also examine specific cases of low-mass binary systems, including those with white dwarfs and those that undergo a mass transfer episode.  Finally, we outline the potential for future research, focusing on the inclusion of additional physics and the application of the tool to specific binary systems.  We anticipate that the distinction between neutron star and black hole systems will be confirmed through repeated observations of their merger timescales, and we discuss the feasibility of achieving this goal.  We further investigate the possibility of utilizing the spin-induced orbital decay feature in certain low-mass binary systems as a distinguishing marker.  We conclude that the most effective approach involves a combination of theoretical analysis, observational data, and the utilization of various astrophysical and gravitational wave indicators.  We aim to eliminate any stigma associated with the uncertainty regarding the nature of LISA binary systems, encouraging the scientific community to view it as a distinctive characteristic rather than a source of concern.  We believe that the uncertainty reflects a mark of distinction, given the impressive sensitivity of LISA and the in-depth understanding of the underlying physics.  We hope that this perspective will contribute to a more positive and constructive discussion on the topic.  We also outline the implications of this perspective, emphasizing the importance of treating the uncertainty as a variable that can be exploited in the search for new physics.  We propose the use of a novel parameter, dubbed the "mass uncertainty factor," to quantify the uncertainty regarding the nature of LISA binary systems.  We demonstrate that this parameter is essential for developing a comprehensive theory of binary system evolution, incorporating multiple formation pathways, distinct physics mechanisms, and diverse theoretical models.

In order to investigate the complexities of doubles play, we developed a mathematical model that automates the evaluation of doubles strategies.   particularly in transient execution attacks like Spectre and Variant attacks.
  Although existing research has focused on mitigating these vulnerabilities,
  our study aims to explore the theoretical foundations of transient execution side-channel attacks.
  We begin by outlining a general framework for analyzing these attacks, which we then use to establish necessary conditions for their success. 
  Building on this framework, we identify key factors that contribute to the variation in attack performance across different variants. 
  We also derive a unified metric to quantify the information leakage in transient execution side-channel attacks, which we found to be non-equivalent to existing entropy-based measures. 
  Our research provides a comprehensive understanding of transient execution side-channel attacks, which we believe will be invaluable in developing effective countermeasures. 
  We further contribute several original findings on the relationships between cache eviction and memory access patterns, which we hope will inspire future research. 
  Our study's findings on the performance boundaries of Variant attacks are particularly intriguing, and we propose several novel exploitation scenarios that bypass established performance limits. 
  Our research demonstrates that even subtle performance differences can significantly impact information leakage, and we identify several hardware optimization opportunities that further reduce performance margins. 
  Our overall goal is to establish a robust theoretical foundation for transient execution side-channel attack analysis, which we achieve through a series of innovative experiments on three distinct Variant attacks. 
  Our results on Branch Target Prediction-based attacks show that by simply reconfiguring hardware settings, we can substantially reduce performance margins and consequently information leakage. 
  We further demonstrate that by combining hardware optimizations with software-based mitigations, we can effectively eliminate information leakage in BTB-based attacks. 
  Our research on Indirect Branching-based attacks reveals that by simply inverting memory access patterns, we can transform performance-critical instructions that contribute to information leakage into non-performance-critical ones that do not. 
  Our overall objective is to contribute to the development of a comprehensive side-channel attack taxonomy, which we achieve by outlining a general framework for classifying information leakage mechanisms. 
  We believe that our research will have a lasting impact on the construction of robust security models and the design of efficient countermeasures against transient execution side-channel attacks. 
  We make all of our code and data available on a public repository for the benefit of the security community.  No ethics approval was required for this research. Despite its intriguing characteristics, understanding the DPO state's microscopic origins has been challenging due to the complexity of theoretical models and the scarcity of experimental data.  This study uses neutron scattering experiments to provide a detailed picture of the DPO state in the perovskate irridate compound SrIrO3.  By analyzing the spin excitation spectrum, we find evidence that local and non-local exchange interactions are crucial in describing the DPO state.  A theoretical model, consistent with ab initio calculations, reveals that the long-wavelength, low-energy excitation is a non-local, bond-centered octupole, while the high-energy excitation is a local, octupolar moment.  Our results offer a comprehensive understanding of the DPO state and its implications for the compound's magnetic and ground state properties.  We find that the non-local exchange interactions stabilize the non-collinear, long-wavelength magnetic structure, whereas the local exchange interactions determine the local, high-energy octupolar moments.  Furthermore, we observe a direct correlation between the non-local exchange interactions and the DPO state's characteristics, allowing us to predict its behavior in strained SrIrO3.  This research provides a fundamental framework for exploring the DPO state in perovskate irridate compounds and offers insights for designing materials with unique magnetic properties.  It also paves the way for investigating other materials with similar spin excitation spectra, such as the perovskate osmate compound SrOsO3.  This study's findings are expected to contribute to a broader understanding of transition metal oxides' magnetic behavior and their potential applications in spin-based technologies. This research is based on 1.0 fb$^{-1}$ of $p$p collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, recorded by the LHCb experiment. As the decay products of charmed hadrons are produced in their rest frame, their azimuthal correlations provide a framework for studying the alignment of heavy mesons within their parent protons. Observations of large gaps in some disks, such as the FOMALM and HL Tauri systems, suggest that some areas have already formed into notable planets.  However, the formation mechanism of inner gaps and the role of giant planets in disk evolution remain unclear.  This research aims to investigate the relationship between protoplanetary disks and planet formation using computer simulations of the radial distribution of dust particles and gas in disks.  By simulating the effects of giant planets on disk structure, we can determine whether observed large gaps in disks are indicative of massive planetary presence or alternative formation processes.  As massive planets can easily remove dust within their vicinity, causing large gaps to form, we can assess their potential role in driving the formation of water and rocky planets in their orbit.  Additionally, we can explore how giant planet formation occurs in relation to the growth of small particles and the development of ring systems in disks.  This study contributes to our understanding of how planetary systems evolve and form, providing a framework for analyzing future observations of protoplanetary disks and the search for evidence of forming planets through missions like the James Webb Space Telescope.  It also explores the potential for massive planets to influence the formation of rocky worlds in distant orbits and the potential for their discovery through transit and radial velocity observations.  This research paves the way for a new standard model of planetary system development, focusing on the pivotal role of giant planets in shaping the composition and structure of rocky worlds. This modified state, called the "pair-density wave" (PDW) state, takes into account the spatial arrangements of pairs of electrons. We derive an expression for the PDW ground state within a microscopic framework, focusing on a specific model that incorporates interactions and lattice effects. By applying this framework to a lattice gas model, we demonstrate that the PDW state emerges as the most stable state when the interaction strength exceeds a certain threshold. Furthermore, we show that this state exhibits distinct Fermi surface breakdowns, which align with the proposed real-space arrangement of electron pairs. We also analyze how the PDW state affects the quasiparticle spectra, revealing a gap opening at points that correspond to the pair arrangement and a closing at other broken Fermi surface segments. Additionally, we examine how the PDW state responds to external stimuli in the form of impurities and phonons, observing its resilience to certain types of disturbances but vulnerability to others. Lastly, we outline the implications of our findings for our understanding of high temperature superconductivity in cuprates and other similar materials, highlighting the challenge of achieving a $d$-wave gap within a single-band model. We conclude by suggesting that the PDW state offers a promising theoretical approach to explaining the unique properties of high temperature superconductors, particularly the opening of a $d$-wave gap and the appearance of nodal behaviors in the spectrum of quasiparticles. We further propose that this state might be realized in materials that exhibit a specific real-space arrangement of electron pairs, such as the checkerboard pattern observed in $1/3$-filled cubic lattices. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of the PDW theory in understanding the electrical and magnetic properties of superconducting materials and other related phenomena. a system with many particles is a significant challenge.
  This challenge makes it difficult to predict the behavior of complex many-particle systems within a quantum mechanical context.
  As a result, even the most basic properties of such systems remain poorly understood.
  A common approach in many-body physics is to utilize a specific particle to develop a framework and then generalize it to account for multiple particles. 
  This approach is based on the principle of equal probability for different measurement outcomes of that particle.
  By applying this principle in conjunction with the concept of Slater determinants, we derive a concise framework for predicting the overall behavior of these systems. 
  This derivation occurs without the need for numerous computational simulations.
  As an example, we explore a scenario where two particles interact with a pre-existing state, and demonstrate that the framework aligns with established expectations. 
  We also extend the scenario to include multiple particles occupying the same energy level, and derive a fundamental property of many-particle states in a confined harmonic oscillator system. 
  This property pertains to the antisymmetrization of wave functions, which is a hallmark of fermionic behavior. 
  We further analyze the probability of detecting particles in close proximity to one another within a one-dimensional box, and derive the distribution of their relative positions. 
  Finally, we apply the framework to a more complex situation involving multiple particles in a box that is connected to a harmonic oscillator, and explore different possible state configurations. 
  This comprehensive approach provides a clear foundation for investigating various aspects of many-particle systems, and has far-reaching applications in fields such as atomic physics, condensed matter physics, and chemical physics. 
  This tutorial review is designed to be self-contained, and targets readers with a solid grasp of fundamental quantum mechanics principles. 
  We assume no prior knowledge of many-body theory and focus on developing a clear, intuitive understanding of underlying concepts and frameworks. 
  Throughout the material, we emphasize the intrinsic physical significance of various mathematical formulations and derivations. 
  We also include numerous illustrative examples, along with a collection of useful appendices that offer supplementary information on relevant theoretical topics. 
  This review is intended to serve as a starting point for further exploration of many-particle systems, and aims to facilitate the development of a unified, experimentally grounded understanding of these systems. 
  This research is a significant expansion on our previous work, and was made possible by the valuable feedback and suggestions from our peers.

We examine the potential formation of primordial black holes in a scenario where the universe's initial conditions were non-singular and featured a gentle beginning, potentially taking the form of a "little big bang."  A phase of rapid cooling might occur in such a scenario, and we calculate the resulting primordial black hole mass ranges using an extended version of the Press-Schechter formalism.  Considering a universe composed mainly of dark matter, we find that primordial black holes of significant abundance would be created if the initial gentle inflation lasted for at least 60 e-folds, with further formation possible through phase transitions.  We also investigate the possible impact of primordial black holes on the universe's composition, including their potential role in seed galaxies, the formation of heavy elements, and their possible abundance in certain mass ranges.  Finally, we discuss the potential observational evidence for primordial black holes of small masses, including their possible role in opening star formation pathways in gas, their contribution to metal enrichment in gases, and their possible connection to gamma-ray burst mechanisms. Throughout the paper, we highlight the importance of considering various formation theories and formation mechanisms when evaluating primordial black hole formation, as well as the need for a multi-faceted understanding of the phenomenon. Our method, called the Persistent Random Walk (PRW), builds upon the persistent walk framework by allowing for abrupt changes in direction that occur at unpredictable, stationary points. Processed data in the form of images and videos is metadata, and its massive accumulation creates opportunities for both the genuine scientific purpose and the malicious intent behind data collection. With the line between these purposes often blurred, there is a growing concern that excessive data collection could compromise the integrity of research. By establishing a clear framework for understanding the relationship between video-based metadata and research outcomes, this paper aims to facilitate a more nuanced discussion about the subject and to promote the development of transparent, optimized data collection strategies. Unlike previous theories, ours doesn't rely on small amplitude waves, enabling the creation of a composite stability theory that integrates Kelvin-Helmholtz and Rayleigh instabilities. This model is called the Neural Network PDE Model and it essentially solves the PDE by finding the representation of its operator in a linear vector space. This representation is then computed using multilayer neural networks for the linear components and is combined to form the solution. What makes this model particularly effective is its ability to deal with both non-local and nonlinear PDEs by enabling the representation of integral operators and the composition of linear representatives. This representation learning approach allows for the direct solution of PDEs without the need for a discretized space and has been demonstrated to outperform traditional finite difference methods in various tests. This success suggests potential applications in large-scale PDE simulations. This work also introduces a regularization technique that suppresses trivial representations and enhances the model's performance. This regularization is frame-independent and can be combined with other methods for further improvement. This regularization technique is based on a frame of radial basis functions centered in the unity ball and has been found to yield the best results in the tests conducted. This regularization is also reusable and can be used in combination with other methods for further improvement. This work also explores the theoretical aspects of the Neural Network PDE Model by demonstrating its accuracy, examining the optimization process, and analyzing the representation stability. This stability is essential for the regularization as it guarantees its effectiveness. This stability is also desirable for other regularization methods. This stability is based on a series of norm inequalities for the representation of the operator and has been proven for both bounded and unbounded operators in both compact and non-compact domains. This stability is applicable in various contexts by enabling the computation of the operator representation at points in the unity ball that are close to a manifold with a boundary that is known in advance. This stability is also applicable in the regularization technique mentioned earlier. This work further contributes the development of a specific implementation of the Neural Network PDE Model that is called the Fourier Neural Network PDE Model for PDEs with constant coefficients. This implementation is particularly effective for PDEs with periodic symbols and has been found to yield the best results in the tests conducted. This effectiveness is due to the Fourier transforms that enable the representation of harmonic operators as products of representations of their variables' frequencies. This effectiveness is also desirable for other implementations as it provides a general framework that can be combined with other methods for further improvement. The detection of cosmic microwave background radiation anisotropies by satellite-based experiments has allowed us to map these initial imbalances, providing a clear picture of how these fluctuations evolved over time.  As we continue to refine our instruments, upcoming missions such as CMB-S4 are expected to significantly improve our capabilities, enabling us large-scale universe structure data that is sensitive to minor fluctuations of order $10^{-10}$.  With this heightened precision, we may be able to discern the signature of massive neutrinos within the universe through their impact on structure formation, particularly in the form of a blueshift in the spectrum of eos-like matter-radiation universes or a shift in the scale factor at which the universe's density transitioned from radiation to matter. We present an approach for reconstructing the initial condition of a linear wave equation, with an unknown boundary that is partially hidden from observation. By utilizing a linear operator derived from the Neumann-to-Dirichlet operator, we are able to reconstruct the initial condition within an accuracy of order $\epsilon$ using a data volume of order $1/\epsilon^2$. This reconstruction is stable, meaning it is insensitive to noise of order less than $\epsilon$. This reconstruction is also theoretically validated for any choice of observerable boundary, as well as one that is curved, inhomogeneous, and/or moving. The reconstruction procedure is also optomized in terms of data volume, with an upper bound of order $1/\epsilon$ in the case of a point-wise reconstruction. We also explore the stability of the Neumann-to-Dirichlet operator, demonstrating that it can be represented as a linear composition of two boundary integral operators, with their associated regularity properties. We further derive the reconstruction procedure using these operators, along with an approximation scheme that meets the stability requirements. The main theoretical results are further validated using a numerical example, demonstrating the effectiveness of the reconstruction procedure. We also explore the real-time monitoring of a hidden boundary in a real-world scenario of a gas flow in a turbine, demonstrating the practical utility of the reconstruction procedure. We append three technical appendices, providing further details on the theoretical derivations. We intend for this research to contribute to the development of an imaging technique for the real-time monitoring of a hidden boundary in various physical scenarios, as well as the design of numerical algorithms for its implementation. This achieves an important milestone in the field of inverse problems for a linear wave equation, as previously believed that an infinite amount of observable information was required for a boundary with a complex shape.  This research overcomes this limitation by utilizing a linear operator derived from the Neumann-to-Dirichlet operator, which is capable of reconstructing a boundary with a curvature of order $1/\epsilon^3$ using a data volume of order $1/\epsilon^2$. We demonstrate that in statistical experiments, the information gathered is not a function of outcomes but rather of the measurement process itself. We derive the main result that the information gained from an experiment can be zero at the outset, regardless of the precision of the measurement tools employed. a gas giant planet like Jupiter is crucial, particularly when considering its internal dynamics, composition, and formation history.  While seismic data has reshaped our knowledge of Earth's internal structure, a similar capacity to probe Jupiter's interior is lacking due to the planet's gas state precluding seismic activity.  As a result, the giant planet's interior structure remains poorly defined, with conflicting models proposed based on limited data from Jupiter's gravitational and magnetic fields, as well as exterior mass distribution information.  We aim to rectify this knowledge gap by exploring the possible connection between the composition and temperature profiles of a gas giant planet and its intrinsic oscillation modes, considering both linear adiabatic stability criteria and the way oscillations occur in the planet.  Using a 1D hydrostatic planetary model and assuming a composition consisting primarily of hydrogen and helium, we developed a novel approach to determine the distinct layers of a gas giant planet based on the oscillation frequency data from seismic models.  We integrated the Euler-Poisson equation to derive the native oscillation modes of a gas giant planet, subject to the adiabatic stability condition and the Brunt-Väisälä frequency boundary criterion.  We found that the native inversion eigenfrequencies are directly linked to the temperature profile around the chemical composition boundaries, allowing for a clear determination of the inner rock core size in a Jupiter-like planet.  We believe that the Brunt-Väisälä frequency boundary criterion is essential for validating the planetary interior models, as it guarantees the linear stability of the native oscillation modes.  We further established that the native oscillation modes are primarily affected by the temperature profile around the metallicity boundaries, rather than the overall pressure and temperature conditions.  We propose that the Brunt-Väisälä frequency profile could serve as a valuable indicator for identifying the layers of a gas giant planet based on observational data from its gravitational field, as it is closely correlated with the native inversion eigenfrequencies.  We conclude that the intrinsic oscillation modes of a gas giant planet offer a novel, composition-independent method for determining its interior structure, complementing other approaches based on gravity and magnetic field data.  We outline the potential for this method to be utilized with future missions capable of detecting Jupiter's intrinsic oscillation modes through gravity measurements, as well as the development of observational strategies for identifying the Brunt-Väisälä frequency profile based on data from missions like the Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer (JUICE) and the Europa Clipper. observed in the galaxy NGC 1068 is filled by a hot, dense accretion disk atmosphere, which produces the notable 10-30 keV iron fluorescence feature detected in its spectrum. Our analysis utilizes a model of the geometry of the system, specifically one that incorporates the centrally located black hole and the bulge of the galaxy. We account for the effects of relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations on the disk's structure, specifically those that describe the behavior of gas and magnetic fields at 10 r_g^-1 <= alpha <= 30 r_g^-1, where r_g is the gravitational radius. We find that a disk atmosphere, heated by X-rays that precipitate from the black hole's vicinity, can indeed yield the observed fluorescence feature. What is more, we determine that this specific configuration is not unique, and that multiple parameter sets can produce a similar outcome. Ultimately, our results support the alternative view that the cavity is not a vacuum, but rather a region depleted of cold gas, which is resistant to X-ray illumination. This conclusion is based on the production of the 10-30 keV fluorescence feature in a different physical scenario for each parameter set examined. The overall implications of our findings for the mass return rate of the gas in the disc cavity are also explored.   Based on the data available at the time of the research, the 10-30 keV fluorescence feature in the NGC 1068 spectrum cannot be fully reproduced by a simple, slab-like disk atmosphere. A more complex geometry, possibly one that involves a torus, is necessary to account for the observed levels of fluorescence. This is particularly true for the harder energy bands (>15 keV), which are not produced by a standard, Compton-thick disk atmosphere. A more elaborate structure, one that allows for the buildup of a significant iron K-beta feature, is also essential for describing the behavior of the iron L lines in the spectrum.   A team of researchers used a physical model of the accretion disk atmosphere to investigate the relationship between the 10-30 keV iron fluorescence feature and the mass return rate of gas in the disc cavity of NGC 1068. Two different scenarios were explored: one in which the dust sublimation front was close to the central black hole, and another in which the front was farther away. In both cases, a hotter, denser disk atmosphere was found to produce a stronger fluorescence feature. What is more, the models indicated a positive correlation between the mass return rate and the production of the fluorescence

for classical first-order logic stems from the completeness theorem for matrix systems, particularly for classical modal logic, which in turn derives from the completeness theorem for Boolean algebras. We aim to provide a new proof of the completeness theorem for classical first-order logic, drawing on the completeness theorem for finite identity matrix systems of modal logic, rather than the classical completeness theorem for first-order logic. We achieve this by integrating the method of Lindenbach's polynomial approximation, originally used in the context of point-free modal topology, into our proof. This approach enables a representation of (finite) structures through identity-free modal semantics, thereby establishing a connection between structure-based and semantics-based approaches to first-order logic. Our proof yields a decision procedure for validity in finite structures, by combining the completeness theorems for modal logic and the capacity for solving identity equations over finite structures. We further demonstrate that this approach is equivalent to the method of Gro\"bler, Otto, and Tschietsch, and that it outperforms it in terms of computational complexity. We provide conditions on the occurring sequences of matrices that guarantee the convergence of the recursive average to a limit, in the form of a linear system of equations. We also demonstrate that these conditions are sufficient for the convergence of the recursive average in a probability space. Building on these results, we show that the recursive average can be represented as a linear integral with respect to the underlying measure, if that measure is regular. Under the assumption of a regular measure, we prove that the limit of the recursive average is invariant to the choice of initial vector, as long as the sequence of matrices is ergodic with respect to the measure. If the measure is finite, we establish that the limit of the recursive average is unique. We further show that the limit of the recursive average is equal to the stationary distribution of the linear dynamics described by the matrix sequence, under the assumption of a stationary measure. Finally, we extend our findings to settings where the updates use a weighted average of multiple vector averages, and we outline possible applications and extensions. We present a dynamic framework that incorporates sequential decisions, stochastic processes, and information lag, and show an integral representation for the value function. We obtain a key result showing that the value function has a closed-form expression in the case of a binary outcome, which enables the derivation of an optimal strategy. Our approach leads to a characterization of the optimal action at each stage through a system of integral equations, which can be solved using a specific discretization scheme. We further develop a numerical algorithm based on this scheme and provide an analysis of its computational complexity. We demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness by solving several test problems and show its applicability to a variety of outcomes distributions. We also investigate the algorithm's performance in scenarios with multiple actions at each stage and outcomes with varying levels of uncertainty. We further extend our framework to a repeated multi-stage decision-making process and provide an integral representation for the stationary occupant strategy. We apply our framework to a model of pollution control and show that a cooperative equilibrium can be achieved through a combination of conservation efforts and market-based mechanisms. We believe that our paper contributes to our knowledge of dynamic decision-making processes and offers practical solutions for various real-world problems. define a new metric in the space of probability distributions and investigate its key properties.  This metric, called the $2$-Wasserstein metric, exhibits gradual growth as the underlying distance between points increases, meeting the requirements for a metric in the classical sense.  By leveraging a fundamental result from Brunk, we establish that this metric induces equivalent relationships in the space of probability distributions within a given bounded domain.  Building on this, we demonstrate the $2$-Wasserstein metric's uniqueness in this context.  Furthermore, we explore a key embedding theorem for metrics derived from mass transport, including the $2$-Wasserstein metric, by incorporating tools from Gromov's metric embedding theory. We demonstrate that in a Musielak metric space, a function belongs to the vMO class if its distributional derivative is weak-* vMO. We also establish that functions with vanishing Riemann mean oscillation are equivalent to functions whose distributional derivatives are weak-* vMO. We further prove that in a Musielak metric space, a function belongs to the vMO class if its distributional derivative is a member of the Lorentz space $h^1$. Our findings contribute to the development of vMO theory in metric spaces, offering a framework for analyzing functions with negligible mean behavior in diverse geometric settings. Our approach also provides a tool for investigating harmonic functions in potential theory and the vMO criterion for harmonic functions in the context of a specific fractal graph. We then introduce the idea of compact embedded operator spaces within the context of free probability and explain how compact right ideals in a C*-regular hypergroup serve as a foundation for constructing such spaces.  We demonstrate that the compact embedded operator space framework generalizes both the compact interpolation spaces of a hypergroup and the compact subspaces of an operator space that are invariant under the GNS construction.  We also outline the key steps in developing a theory of Fock spaces within the free probability framework, focusing on the case of a single creation operator.  Finally, we outline the approach for constructing antilinear maps (referred to as "creation operators" in the introductory context) within the free probability framework and explain how these constructions enable the formation of regularized products.  Throughout the paper, we highlight the necessity of employing a compact embedded operator space framework to avoid issues with divergent expectations and infinitely large values.  The paper aims to contribute to the growing body of research on free probability theory in relation to operator spaces, and we anticipate that the compact embedded operator space framework will facilitate novel applications and discoveries.  One such potential area of exploration involves utilizing the framework to investigate the second moment of a matrix-valued free Poisson process.  We also outline the potential for future studies on the construction of anti-linear maps in the context of free cumulants and the development of a free probability theory for creation operators in hypergroups.  We have made a conscious decision to focus on the fundamental construction of the compact embedded operator space framework and its underlying theory, leaving the exploration of specific examples to future research.  We have included a comprehensive appendix providing a detailed account of the key technical ingredients, including right ideals, operator spaces, C*-hypergroups, Fock spaces, creation operators, antilinear maps, and free probability theory.  We believe that this paper paves the way for a broader narrative on the free probability theory of creation operators in hypergroups, which we intend to explore in a potential follow-up study.  One of the paper's key contributors, Ben A. Buermann, passed away in 2019, and we have chosen to publish this work in its current form in his memory.  Buermann's research on free probability theory in relation to operator spaces was highly regarded within the academic community, and we hope that this paper will honor his legacy by contributing to the development of this area of research

In a multiple measurement scenario, this challenge intensifies exponentially with the number of measurements.  We demonstrate that an unambiguous determination of the Hamiltonian is not possible beyond a certain point, regardless of any enhancement from the system's dynamics.  This limit corresponds to the number of distinct outcomes observable in the system, and it has no connection to the system's quantum characteristics.  As a result, it marks the fundamental boundary beyond which the mark of distinguishability is lost, forcing a blending of distinct Hamiltonians into a single effective one.  We derive this limit theoretically and validate it through a concrete example.  It is worthy of note that this limit only concerns the reconstruction of the Hamiltonian's real portion.  Upon a system's decay, the imaginary portion emerges, and its reconstruction is significantly more manageable.
